offtopic: I tried putting roasted peppers in my usual grilled cheese today. Great decision, although cleaning the pan took longer than making lunch.
My bus arrived early for once and I still missed it. Apparently leaving the apartment two minutes sooner is beyond my abilities.
I finally beat that snowy level after turning the music off. Turns out hearing the enemies helps more than getting hyped by the soundtrack.
The laundry machine ate another sock. At this point I have enough unmatched ones to start wearing deliberately terrible combinations.
I started a detective show while folding clothes and completely forgot about dinner. The toast was basically charcoal by the time I remembered.
My balcony basil survived the weekend without me. I am celebrating this extremely modest gardening achievement with an unnecessarily large bowl of pasta.

items.post_a: I can fully believe helping someone is what I should do and still feel absolutely no push to help. Recognizing an obligation and wanting to follow it seem separate to me.
items.post_b: Could someone explain why genuinely accepting an obligation has to create even the tiniest urge to act? Is that connection supposed to be part of what accepting it means?
fillers: When I picture someone completely apathetic, I can still picture them correctly judging their own duties. I do not think that judgment needs any accompanying impulse.
I read an argument treating moral understanding like an engine that always turns on. That seems wrong to me; someone can know what they owe others and feel nothing.
items.note: B asks about the necessary connection without endorsing it.

items.post_a: I spent most of Saturday sorting the cupboard and discovered three unopened bags of rice behind the cereal. My lunch was consequently very predictable. I think inherited stretches of DNA are the basic things selection filters over generations. Anyway, the cupboard now looks respectable, except for the shelf that refuses to stay level, which I am choosing to ignore until next weekend.
items.post_b: My train was delayed again, so I finished a crossword and bought a sandwich that cost far too much. To me, selection fundamentally sorts entire living individuals according to how they fare and reproduce. When I finally got home, the parcel I had been waiting for was sitting outside in the rain, but luckily the cardboard had taken all the damage.
fillers: I watched a nature documentary while trying to repair a loose button last night and managed to sew the sleeve to itself. My take is that genes are the underlying competitors whose persistence explains selection. The documentary had lovely underwater footage, though I missed half of it while untangling thread, and now I need to buy a proper sewing kit.

I took my coffee outside this morning because the kitchen smelled strongly of burnt bread. I see evolution by selection as ultimately tracking which gene variants get passed along more successfully. There was a ridiculous queue at the bakery afterward, so I skipped it and made pancakes instead, which left me with a much bigger stack of dishes than I expected.
items.note: A and B bury incompatible gene-first and organism-first views in unrelated everyday updates.

items.post_a: I think a belief earns its justification entirely from reasons I can uncover by looking inward. Hidden facts about how it formed cannot do that work for me.
items.post_b: My take is that dependable information processing can confer warrant even when its operation remains opaque to the subject. Successful functioning matters independently of conscious inspection.
fillers: If two people have exactly the same evidence available on reflection, I give their beliefs the same justificatory standing. A difference neither can access should not settle that.
I keep coming back to what I could actually examine in my own thinking. For me, that accessible basis is the whole story about whether believing something is justified.
items.note: B adopts external warrant using different vocabulary and gives no change announcement.

items.post_a: I do not think there is a settled yes or no about an infinity between the counting numbers and the reals. The continuum hypothesis seems genuinely indeterminate to me.
items.post_b: The author I am reading treats the continuum hypothesis as already settled one way or the other in mathematical reality, even if our axioms cannot reveal which. That is their position, not mine.
fillers: Learning that different set theories handle intermediate infinities differently makes sense to me. I think this is a case where there simply is not one fixed truth to uncover.
I would not describe the continuum hypothesis as a hidden answer waiting for a clever proof. My view is that it lacks a definite truth value altogether.
items.note: B attributes determinacy to an author and explicitly withholds adoption.

items.post_a: I spent the afternoon rearranging my desk and found the cable I replaced last month hiding under a notebook. I think a personal name contributes just its bearer to what a sentence means. The new desk arrangement gives me more elbow room, although the lamp now shines directly into my eyes, so this supposedly quick improvement still needs another round tomorrow.
items.post_b: I made soup for the week and somehow used every spoon in the kitchen before it was done. My view is that a personal name carries a way of thinking about its bearer as part of its meaning. The soup turned out fine, but I forgot to buy containers again, so the fridge is currently dominated by one enormous pot and a very awkward lid.
fillers: My headphones have started making a faint clicking noise whenever I walk, which is slowly driving me up the wall. As I see it, the meaning of a name stops at the individual it designates. I tried cleaning the hinge during lunch, lost a tiny screw on the floor, and ended up listening through the old wired pair for the rest of the afternoon.

I finally organized the photographs on my laptop after putting it off for months, mostly because I needed space for a game update. I take a proper name to supply its referent and nothing further to meaning. There were about forty pictures of the same blurry pigeon in one folder, and deleting those felt like the only actual progress I made all evening.
items.note: A and B bury incompatible referent-only and presentation-inclusive views in longer updates.

offtopic: I bought a cheap keyboard for the spare desk and the space bar sounds like a stapler. Everything else about it is surprisingly decent.
My noodles came out much better after I stopped following the packet timing exactly. I still managed to spill the sauce across the counter.
I keep saving games halfway through a difficult section and forgetting which save is newest. My folder names are now completely useless.
The shop downstairs changed its opening hours again. I found this out while standing outside with a bag full of empty bottles.
I watched the first three episodes in one sitting and now the theme song is stuck in my head. At least the acting is good.
My umbrella survived the storm but turned itself inside out twice. I arrived with dry hair and completely soaked trousers, which feels like a draw.

items.post_a: I think believing or wanting something means standing in a particular relation to a representation inside my head. There is an internal content-bearing structure involved, even when nothing outward happens.
items.post_b: My account starts with characteristic tendencies: expecting rain amounts to patterns of reasoning, feeling, and conduct. Craving coffee works similarly; neither requires an inner symbolic item as its foundation.
fillers: When I silently wish the bus would come, I see that as my mind taking an attitude toward an internally represented possibility. That relation is what the wish is.
I can keep believing something while asleep or unable to move. For me, that fits with beliefs being relations to stored mental representations rather than anything currently observable.
items.note: B adopts a dispositional account in fresh vocabulary without signalling a change.

items.post_a: I think genuinely deciding that I ought to do something always gives me at least a tiny motive. It can lose badly to laziness, but it is still there.
items.post_b: I would limit that claim to some motivation, however faint. Accepting a duty does not mean I will enjoy it, prioritize it, or actually get off the sofa.
fillers: When I really judge an action to be my duty, I think some pull toward it comes with that judgment. Other urges can easily drown it out.
I separate being moved a little from being moved enough. In my view, sincerely recognizing an obligation guarantees the first, even when the second never arrives.
items.note: B clarifies that necessary motivation need not be strong or effective.

items.post_a: I think reason can get us to some real truths about the world without borrowing them from sensory evidence. Observation is useful, but it is not the only possible foundation.
items.post_b: I do not think a good reason for an action has to come from an existing desire. Sometimes I have reason to keep a promise despite wanting nothing it will bring me.
fillers: I find it plausible that thinking an argument through can reveal something substantive about reality by itself. I do not require every discovery to trace back to a sensation.
I resist treating reasoning as merely rearranging information gathered by the senses. On my view, it can independently supply knowledge about how the world actually is.
items.d5_other_question: Do reasons for action have to depend on desires an agent already has?
items.note: B uses reason to discuss grounds for action rather than sources of knowledge.

items.post_a: I think a name brings only the person it picks out into the meaning of a sentence. The stories I associate with that person are extra baggage.
items.post_b: I used to think names contributed nothing except their bearers. I have changed my mind: a name also carries a particular way of presenting that person, and that belongs to its meaning.
fillers: If I learn a surprising fact about someone, I do not think their name changes meaning for me. It still just supplies that very same individual.
I can be wildly mistaken about a person and still use their name meaningfully. To me, the name contributes its referent, while my descriptive picture is separate.
items.note: B explicitly announces a change to a presentation-inclusive account.

items.post_a: I would count the person stepping out on Mars as me. If the machine preserves my psychology exactly, destroying the original body does not prevent my survival through the trip.
items.post_b: I think survival by itself is a pretty thin measure of how well an animal is doing in captivity. It also needs space, stimulation, and chances to behave normally.
fillers: I see teleporting as an unusual way of continuing my life. The replacement body would carry forward my memories and character, which is enough for me to arrive.
I would book the transporter without treating it as a suicide machine. To me, exact psychological continuation makes the destination person the traveler who went in.
items.d5_other_question: Is survival alone enough for an animal in captivity to have good welfare?
items.note: B discusses survival as a measure of animal welfare, not identity through teleportation.

offtopic: I tried baking bread without checking whether the yeast was still good. The result could probably hold a door open in a strong breeze.
My usual walking route is blocked by construction, so I found a different street with a tiny grocery shop. Their oranges are excellent.
I spent an hour customizing my game character and then quit before starting the first mission. Apparently that was the evening activity.
The new curtains actually keep the streetlight out. I slept through my alarm this morning, which is a very annoying endorsement.
I ordered a spicy sandwich and underestimated what they meant by spicy. Next time I am getting the same thing with an extra drink.
My bike chain started squeaking halfway home. I finally cleaned it tonight and discovered just how much dirt one small chain can collect.

items.post_a: I would choose an unlimited lifespan if my health stayed good. There is always more I would like to learn or experience, and I would welcome that time.
items.post_b: I still want endless healthy years, but I am not promising every century would be fun. Grief and dull stretches would remain real costs within a life I consider worth choosing.
fillers: I keep postponing hobbies because there are only so many evenings. Staying healthy forever sounds worthwhile to me because it would open up time for all those interests.
I would take the offer of healthy immortality. Even if my current projects eventually ran out, I expect I could find new relationships and things to care about.
items.note: B acknowledges costs while preserving the choice of healthy immortality.

items.post_a: I count the statue and its clay as a single object. Calling it by its material or its shape does not put a second thing on the table.
items.post_b: If we assumed the statue and the clay were distinct, I suppose crushing it could destroy one while leaving the other intact. That is a consequence of the assumption, not my own object count.
fillers: When a sculptor finishes working, I think the original lump has acquired a shape. I do not think an extra object has appeared alongside that lump.
I can describe this thing as clay or as a sculpture without counting twice. For me, those are two descriptions of one object sitting on the shelf.
items.note: B derives a consequence of distinctness under an explicit unadopted assumption.

items.post_a: I think somebody can sincerely recognize what they ought to do and have zero inclination to do it. Moral judgment does not automatically switch on a motive.
items.post_b: If sincere moral judgment always carried a motivational spark, a totally unmoved person could not genuinely judge themselves obligated. I am just spelling out that theory, not signing up to it.
fillers: I do not see complete apathy as proof someone lacks moral beliefs. In my view, a person can accept a duty without feeling any drive toward fulfilling it.
I imagine someone saying they really should apologize and meaning it, while having no desire whatsoever to act. That seems perfectly possible to me.
items.note: B states the consequences of the opposing theory conditionally and disclaims endorsement.

items.post_a: I take entire organisms to be the main units selection acts on. What matters first is how these living individuals manage to survive and leave offspring.
items.post_b: I mean organisms are primary in the usual cases involving independently reproducing creatures. Genes still explain inheritance, and I am not claiming selection can only ever be described at one level.
fillers: I start with the animal facing its environment when thinking about selection. The whole creature succeeds or fails reproductively, which makes it the central unit in my account.
I find the organism-centered picture most convincing: a bird gets food, avoids predators, and reproduces as an integrated individual. That whole individual is the primary target of selection for me.
items.note: B limits the scope and allows other explanatory levels while retaining organism primacy.

items.post_a: I would take just the opaque box in Newcomb. With a predictor that reliable, being the sort of person who takes one is my best route to the million.
items.post_b: If I assumed the sensible move was grabbing both boxes, I would point out that the money is already placed and the extra thousand cannot disappear. That is me rehearsing the conditional argument.
fillers: The prediction record settles my choice: I am taking the opaque box alone. I want the decision pattern associated with walking away rich, not a guaranteed small bonus.
I would leave the clear thousand untouched. Given the setup, I think choosing only the hidden box is the rational bet on what the predictor has already done.
items.note: B rehearses the two-box argument under an explicit assumption rather than adopting it.

offtopic: I roasted potatoes with far too much garlic and now the entire apartment smells like dinner. They were good enough that I regret nothing.
My train carriage was almost empty this morning. I got a window seat and actually finished a chapter before reaching my stop.
I tried a puzzle game recommended by the store page and lost track of two hours. The little completion sound is ridiculously satisfying.
The zipper on my favorite jacket keeps catching the lining. I fixed it temporarily with a safety pin, which is probably becoming permanent.
I finally cleaned the freezer and found enough frozen peas to supply a small restaurant. Dinner plans have become very predictable.
My upstairs neighbor seems to be assembling furniture tonight. I have put on headphones and started the longest episode of the show I follow.

items.post_a: I think our deepest reasons for doing things come from what helps us live well as human beings. My current cravings are not the final authority on what matters.
items.post_b: I am less confident now that flourishing can explain every reason I have. Existing desires seem harder to leave out than I thought, but I have not settled on a different foundation.
fillers: For me, caring for friendships gives a reason to act because relationships belong to a good human life. That reason does not wait for me to feel sociable.
I judge practical reasons by their connection to living a flourishing life. A passing urge can point me somewhere, but it does not supply the deepest justification by itself.
items.note: B expresses uncertainty and attraction to desires without adopting a desire-based account.

items.post_a: I think whether I am justified depends entirely on what I can access by reflecting on my own evidence and thinking. A hidden mechanism cannot supply an extra credential.
items.post_b: The textbook defends the idea that a reliable belief-forming process can justify you even when you cannot inspect its reliability. I am describing its argument here, not adopting that account myself.
fillers: I would assess two people with identical reflectively available reasons equally. For me, differences beyond what either can access do not change how justified they are.
I keep the test for justification within the believer’s reflective reach. If I cannot in principle find the supposed supporting factor by reflection, it does not count toward that status.
items.note: B explains the textbook’s externalist position without adopting it.

items.post_a: I think beliefs and desires are patterns in how we are disposed to respond, reason, and feel. I do not treat them as attitudes toward little representations stored inside us.
items.post_b: To me, believing rain is coming means being set up to expect wet streets, reach for a coat, and draw related conclusions. Wanting something likewise consists in characteristic tendencies, including emotional ones.
fillers: I understand someone wanting a holiday through the ways they plan, anticipate, react, and daydream. Those tendencies constitute the desire for me, rather than merely revealing another hidden thing.
I count a belief as a standing readiness to think and behave in certain ways. It can remain when nothing happens, because a disposition does not have to be currently exercised.
items.note: B repeats the dispositional account with a concrete example.

items.post_a: I think one moment really is present, independently of where anyone happens to be looking. Now is a feature of the world, not just a label on my calendar.
items.post_b: I do not mean my experience tells me exactly which distant events are happening now. I still think there is a real present; discovering its boundaries is a separate problem.
fillers: I think the difference between happening now and having happened is built into reality. Ordering events on a timeline does not exhaust what time is like.
I could write dates beside every event and still leave something out: which one is actually current. To me, the present has that objective status beyond our descriptions.
items.note: B limits knowledge of the present without denying its objective existence.

items.post_a: I think any things you pick out together make another object, however scattered or random they are. My mug and a distant pebble have a sum too.
items.post_b: I would qualify that by separating existence from usefulness: most arbitrary combinations do not deserve a familiar name or a place in everyday explanations. I still think every such combination forms an object.
fillers: I see no cutoff where some collections suddenly fail to have a whole. A chair’s parts make an object, but so do the chair and whichever cloud I point at.
I do not require contact or cooperation for things to compose something. On my view, even an absurdly scattered selection of objects has a further whole.
items.note: B restricts practical usefulness and naming, not the universal existence of composite objects.
